title: Structurally Ordered Cascade-Activatable Fluorescent RNA Probes for Multiplexed Imaging of Endogenous RNAs in Living Cells.
abstract: Sequence-activated fluorescent RNA (FR) probes have emerged as valuable tools for visualizing endogenous RNAs in live cells without the need to genetically modify RNA transcripts. However, the lack of clear guidelines for assembling intramolecular dynamic structure ensembles and integrating multifunctional building blocks into interconnected architectures hinders the development of robust and scalable strategies for sensitive, multiplexed live-cell RNA imaging. Here, we report the development of cascade-activatable FR (CaFR) platform based on a novel, structurally ordered cascade activation strategy. Upon specific recognition of the target RNA, CaFR initiates cascading, domino-like conformational rearrangements that release and reconfigure the interlocked aptamers into their correctly folded, fluorogenic states. CaFR exhibits favourable properties including large dynamic range, high brightness, and excellent scalability, allowing for the robust imaging of endogenous RNAs in both live and fixed cells, even at the single-molecule level. Moreover, Pepper- and Clivia-based CaFR probes are bioorthogonal and enable the simultaneous visualization of two RNAs in live cells. Together, this study provides a generalized strategy to develop high-performance FR probes for the labeling and imaging of endogenous RNA in live cells, which will be useful for understanding the roles of RNA in complex biological processes.

title: Chaperone modulation and the structural basis for sRNA recognition by the conserved ribonuclease YicC.
abstract: The broadly conserved bacterial endoribonuclease YicC represents a widespread but enigmatic family of RNA processing enzymes with poorly defined substrate selectivity. Here, we show that Escherichia coli YicC displays a distinct selectivity, cleaving small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) such as RyhB and RprA but not when they are in complexes with cognate mRNA targets or RNA sponges. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RyhB processing is modulated, but not abolished, by the RNA chaperone Hfq. Our cryo-EM structures of E. coli YicC in apo form and in complexes with substrate and nonsubstrate RNA species capture marked quaternary and tertiary structural switches triggered by sRNA stem-loop binding that engulf and ratchet the RNA into an internal catalytic channel. Structural comparison of cleavable (RyhB) and noncleavable (MicA) sRNA-bound complexes reveal a near-identical ground-state binding mode, proving that cavity docking is sequence-tolerant and decoupled from catalytic execution. Together, our findings suggest that YicC may be a state-selective endoribonuclease and reveal a framework for selective RNA clearance in bacterial posttranscriptional regulation.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: CRISPR-Mediated PABPC1 Upregulation via ELF5 Binding Disruption Enhances Milk Protein and Lipid Biosynthesis in Goat Mammary Epithelial Cells.
abstract: Post-transcriptional control of milk protein and lipid production in goats remains poorly understood. Here we combined ONT full-length transcriptome sequencing with RNA pull-down coupled to LC-MS/MS to identify RNA-binding proteins associated with milk protein mRNAs, and uncovered poly(A)-binding protein cytoplasmic 1 (PABPC1) as a central regulator. PABPC1 bound the 3'UTRs of casein and lipid-related transcripts such as CSN2, CSN3, LALBA, and FASN, stabilizing these mRNAs and promoting their translation, while dose-dependently modulating alternative polyadenylation (APA) site selection to reshape 3'UTR isoform usage. ELF5 directly bound the PABPC1 promoter, repressing its transcription. CRISPR/Cas9 editing of this binding motif relieved this repression, elevating PABPC1 levels and increasing casein accumulation and triglyceride synthesis in goat mammary epithelial cells. Our findings define an ELF5-PABPC1-APA regulatory module and nominate a tractable target for molecular breeding to enhance goat milk protein and lipid content.

title: Efficient design of RNA sequences with desired properties, structure, and motifs using a grammar variational autoencoder.
abstract: Designing structurally stable RNA sequences with specific motifs and other desirable properties is an important challenge in bioinformatics. The potential design space increases exponentially with the length of the RNA to be engineered, making this a difficult combinatorial optimization problem. In this paper, we propose an RNA grammar variational autoencoder (RGVAE) that can efficiently generate novel RNA sequences with specific target properties. The proposed RGVAE builds on the recently proposed grammar VAE, where we incorporate the stochastic context-free grammar (SCFG) to design structural RNAs with desired motifs and characteristics. Using the SCFG can ensure that the generated RNA sequence can form a thermodynamically stable secondary structure. Given a RNA sequence, the SCFG is used to find the parse tree, which is represented in a continuous low-dimensional latent space by the RGVAE encoder. We can optimize the RNA in the latent space, where the latent representation can be decoded by the RGVAE decoder to reconstruct the RNA sequence. Based on a number of practical uses cases, we demonstrate that RGVAE can be used to efficiently design structurally stable RNAs with specific target properties compared to other alternative approaches that do not explicitly incorporate SCFG into the design process. The source code of RGVAE and the data used in this study can be found at: https://github.com/nzarnaghinaghsh/RGVAE.

title: COVID-19 vaccine mRNA and Spike induce cell signaling pathways favoring the growth of tumor cells.
abstract: Copyright: © 2026 Federico. This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY 4.0), which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original author and source are credited. Billions of doses of the mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines have been dispensed worldwide. Vaccine mRNA molecules enter cells due to their complexing with synthetic lipids. Afterwards, the synthetic mRNA translates into a full-length, biologically active, and stabilized form of the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein. Both mRNA and Spike molecules possess intrinsic signaling properties. Vaccine mRNA induces cell responses similar to those elicited by microbial RNA, including the release of downstream soluble factors like IFNα, IFNγ, and IL-6. Spike activates cell signaling pathways, such as those driven by NF-κB, ERK, and AKT, by binding to the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)-2 cell receptor, cell membrane integrins, and other signaling molecules, both intracellularly and extracellularly. This research perspective offers a detailed analysis of the effects on cell signaling induced by both the vaccine mRNA and the Spike protein. A bulk of experimental data supports the idea that these effects, alone and in combination, can switch molecular mechanisms that both directly and indirectly contribute to the neoformation and growth of cancer cells. This possibility calls for additional investigations, considering that, in any case, favoring the growth of tumor cells does not necessarily imply the development of clinically evident tumors, which require additional, still largely unknown conditions.

title: Screening of open-source libraries from the Medicines for Malaria Venture using Bunyamwera virus as a model reveals inhibitors of Oropouche virus infection.
abstract: Arboviral infections remain a major public health concern in tropical and subtropical regions, where environmental and socioeconomic conditions facilitate the circulation of diverse RNA viruses, including over 350 members of the recently renamed Peribunyaviridae family. In this regard, Oropouche virus (OROV) has caused explosive outbreaks in the Amazon region and shows wider distribution in Brazil, with confirmed neurological infections and fatalities in 2024. The absence of effective antiviral therapies highlights an urgent need for the discovery of anti-OROV drugs. In this work, we evaluated the antiviral potential of the Pandemic Response Box and Global Health Priority Box libraries from the Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) against OROV, using a well-established Bunyamwera virus (BUNV) system, widely used as a prototype of the Peribunyaviridae family, expressing the reporter gene enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP). A screening protocol based on fluorescent reporter gene detection by live cell imaging was employed. Nine compounds were identified with significant activity against BUNV-eGFP, with three being highlighted as the most promising hits: Trimetrexate, GSK-983 and MMV1634385. These compounds were validated by testing for activity against OROV, and in these assays, GSK-983 exhibited the lowest EC50 value and consequently the highest selectivity index. Future studies should evaluate the antiviral efficacy of GSK-983 and assess its pharmacokinetic profile. Furthermore, our results indicate that our approach employing BUNV-eGFP as a model against OROV provides an efficient route to prioritize candidate compounds from large libraries, thereby establishing a practical screening route for future antivirals against Oropouche fever.

title: Molecular dynamics simulations for lipid nanoparticles in mRNA delivery: mechanistic insights, evidence limits, and design hypotheses.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading non-viral platform for mRNA delivery, yet the molecular organization and dynamic remodeling events that determine efficiency remain difficult to resolve experimentally. This review critically synthesizes molecular dynamics (MD) studies on mRNA-LNPs and mechanistically informative surrogate systems published from 2020 through April 2026. The literature was organized around the delivery sequence: microfluidic self-assembly, mRNA encapsulation, internal nanostructure, pH-triggered remodeling, endosomal membrane interaction, and cytoplasmic release. Martini 3 coarse-grained simulations, constant-pH and enhanced-sampling strategies, evidence-calibrated interpretation of pH-responsive phase behavior, and mechanism-informed lipid optimization exemplified by Branched Endosomal Disruptor (BEND) lipids are emphasized. Findings demonstrated in intact mRNA-LNPs are distinguished from those inferred from siRNA-LNPs, short RNA oligos, RNA-free mesophases, or model membranes. Current MD has advanced from descriptive visualization to mechanistic hypothesization and design support, but predictive LNP design remains limited by force-field dependence, simplified biointerfaces, limited validation in intact mRNA-LNPs, and the absence of protein-corona models.

title: Decoding neurodegeneration: RNA therapeutics in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.
abstract: Neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease are of major global health concern considering that they are progressive and not curable. The standard therapeutic methods mainly aim at the treatment of the symptoms, and they do not treat the molecular processes that contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease. Over the last few years, RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as a promising approach to precisely target disease-specific genes and pathways at the molecular level. This review examines the involvement of the use of different RNA-based methods such as small interfering RNA (siRNA), microRNA (miRNA), messenger RNA (mRNA) and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in the management of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. The article emphasises the ability of these therapies to regulate gene expression that relates to some of the major pathological phenotypes, including amyloid-beta deposition, hyperphosphorylation of the tau protein, and alpha-synuclein aggregation. In addition to that, it also talks about the progress in delivery systems to address limitations such as the blood-brain barrier, making RNA therapeutics more clinically applicable. The existing evidence of research shows that there is great potential to slow the progression of disease and improve the functioning of neurons. In spite of these developments, there are still some issues such as the problems of stability, off-target effects, and mass production. On the whole, RNA-based therapeutics is an innovative solution that can potentially turn the face of neurodegenerative diseases treatment. These innovations should be translated to effective therapeutic interventions, which can only be achieved through further research and clinical validation.

title: Bdnf mRNA-LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Models.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have rapidly emerged as a transformative approach for treating a range of health challenges. Accelerated by the success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, this platform holds promise beyond immunisation for the transient expression of therapeutic proteins in targeted tissues. Despite this promise, non-invasive delivery of mRNA-encoded cargo to the brain remains a challenge, as most peptide drugs do not pass the blood-brain barrier. Here, we present the development of an intranasal mRNA-LNP therapeutic that drives production of neurotrophic factors in the nasal epithelium and delivery of the encoded protein to the brain. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that intranasal delivery of mRNA encoding the neurogenic factor BDNF (Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor) enhances memory performance in both aged mice and a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. This approach offers a promising platform for delivering therapeutic proteins to the brain and opens new avenues for treating age-related and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Transcriptional Regulation Governed by 7SK-snRNP Complex: Co-Phosphorylation-Guided Implications Through Phosphoproteomics Data Integration of MEPCE.
abstract: Methylphosphate capping enzyme (MEPCE) is a key enzymatic and structural component of the 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex. The complex controls the sequestration of P-TEFb, which regulates transcriptional elongation by phosphorylating RNA polymerase II. Although protein phosphorylation is a regulatory protein modification governing this process, the phosphorylation landscape and signaling association of MEPCE concerning its function remain understudied. Therefore, we performed an integrative mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomics data harmonization through systematic screening of more than 3800 publicly available human phosphoproteomics studies to construct a comprehensive phosphorylation map of MEPCE. Frequency-based prioritization identified six predominant phosphorylation sites of MEPCE, including S69, S152, T213, S216, S217, and S254, which were further characterized through co-regulation profiling, kinase-substrate prediction, functional enrichment analysis, and protein-protein interaction network reconstruction. These multi-layered analyses revealed extensive co-phosphorylation connectivity of MEPCE with proteins involved in RNA polymerase II pause-release and transcription elongation mechanisms conserved across diverse experimental conditions. Analysis showed S152, a phosphorylation site critical for MEPCE activity, exhibited convergence of a large network of 33 co-phosphorylating upstream kinases associated with splicing, co-transcriptional RNA processing, and stimulus-responsive pathways, suggesting integration of extracellular signaling with transcriptional regulation. Interestingly, several hnRNPs, U6 snRNPs, and proteins in the TFIIH holo complex showed co-phosphorylation tendency with MEPCE phosphorylation, further indicating transcription elongation control and post-transcriptional RNA maturation. The findings establish a system-level, proteomics-driven, statistically robust, and replicable framework for understanding potential phosphorylation-dependent regulation of MEPCE. The data extends several testable hypotheses which can be pursued for experimentally elucidating co-phosphoregulatory networks relevant 7SK snRNP-lead mechanisms.

title: Enhanced delivery and antitumor efficacy of CXCR2-targeting siRNA nanoparticles by regulating cancer-associated fibroblasts in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Background: Effective delivery systems for small interfering RNA (siRNA) are crucial for therapeutic gene silencing in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment. Incorporating targeting motifs and stimuli-responsive elements can enhance delivery effectiveness and specificity. Methods: A novel PEI-PBA (PP) nanocomplex was synthesized for siRNA delivery by conjugating polyethylenimine (PEI) with 4-carboxyphenylboronic acid (PBA) through an amide coupling reaction. PP nanocomplexes were evaluated for physical properties, biocompatibility, cellular uptake, and gene silencing efficiency both in vitro using HCC cell lines and in vivo using an HCC mouse model. Results: PP nanocomplexes efficiently encapsulated siRNA and protected it from nuclease degradation. Morphological examinations showed a consistent particle size of approximately 150 nm and good colloidal stability. Significant ATP-responsive siRNA release was confirmed, indicating potential for targeted therapeutic delivery. In vitro, mannose functionalization enhanced cellular uptake and promoted significant lysosomal escape, contributing to effective gene silencing. Specifically, siCXCR2-loaded PP nanocomplexes markedly inhibited CXCR2 gene and protein expression and significantly reduced HCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. In vivo, PP nanocomplexes demonstrated targeted delivery and significant accumulation at tumor sites, resulting in notable tumor growth inhibition, particularly when combined with sorafenib. Conclusion: PP nanocomplexes, especially mannose-functionalized formulations, provide an effective siRNA delivery system with high cell viability, optimal cellular internalization, and potent antitumor activity both in vitro and in vivo, while maintaining favorable physicochemical characteristics and biocompatibility in future therapeutic applications. These findings support further development of this platform for versatile cancer therapy integrating gene silencing with targeted delivery to tumor tissues.

title: Timing of ribosomal RNA modification during eukaryotic ribosome biogenesis.
abstract: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) modifications are critical for ribosome function, influencing rRNA stability, structure, and interactions with ribosomal proteins and transfer RNA. However, the precise timing of modification during the complex process of ribosome biogenesis remains unknown. We address this knowledge gap by analyzing Saccharomyces cerevisiae precursor rRNA (pre-rRNA) through purification of RNA polymerase I and III and Nanopore direct RNA sequencing. Using quantitative RNA modification analyses of distinct pre-rRNA intermediates along the rRNA maturation pathway, we discover the timing of rRNA modifications mediated by small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins (snoRNPs) and other enzymes. All H/ACA snoRNPs act co-transcriptionally to form pseudouridines before 20S and 27SA2 pre-rRNAs are separated, and the same is true for C/D snoRNPs generating 2'-O-methylations. Most modifications, particularly those at the 5' end of 18S rRNA, are fully installed already in 35S pre-rRNA, however certain modifications in the central and 3' regions of 18S rRNA are only completed in later stages of ribosome assembly. These observations indicate that snoRNPs can continue to act on selected sites in pre-rRNA during subsequent pre-ribosome maturation steps. In conclusion, we provide detailed insights into the timing of rRNA modification during the early stages of rRNA maturation and the molecular choreography of eukaryotic ribosome biogenesis.

title: Fully modified SpyCas9 guide RNAs enable robust genome editing in cells and in vivo.
abstract: Precision engineering of CRISPR/Cas9 components has advanced genome editing toward therapeutic applications. Fully chemically modified guide RNAs (gRNAs) have the potential to improve stability and broaden therapeutic delivery strategies. However, extensive chemical modification of CRISPR guides can compromise genome editing activity by disrupting gRNA-Cas9 interactions. Here, we employed an iterative, structure-guided optimization strategy to systematically evaluate chemical modifications throughout SpyCas9 gRNAs. Extending beyond commonly used nucleotide modifications, we incorporated 2'-amino-RNA, 4'-thio-RNA, and extended nucleic acid (exNA) to generate gRNAs in which 90%-100% of nucleotides are sugar- or backbone-modified. Although the performance of individual modification patterns varied among target sequences, we established a repertoire of guides that support robust genome editing in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings provide a systematic framework for rational engineering of heavily and fully modified gRNAs using diverse nucleotide chemistries for nonviral CRISPR genome editing.

title: The complete chloroplast genome of the Korean endemic fern Hypodematium angustifolium C.S. Lee & K.H. Lee (Hypodematiaceae).
abstract: Hypodematium angustifolium, a fern species endemic to Korea, has no reported genomic characteristics or phylogenetic position. In this study, the complete chloroplast genome of H. angustifolium was assembled and characterized: 150,022 bp in length with a typical quadripartite structure. Overall, 128 genes were identified (87 protein-coding genes (PCGs), eight ribosomal RNAs, and 33 transfer RNAs). Additionally, 73 RNA editing sites were predicted. Phylogenetic analysis based on 84 PCGs showed that H. angustifolium was clearly distinguishable from H. crenatum. These genomic data provide a resource for future phylogenetic and evolutionary studies of Hypodematium.

title: METTL16-dependent m⁶A enrichment and GLS1 transcript stability are associated with glutamine-related metabolic changes in hemangioma-derived cells.
abstract: Deciphering how epitranscriptomic regulation coordinates metabolic adaptation requires integrated strategies that connect RNA modification with metabolic and functional phenotypes. Here, we established a systematic framework combining genetic perturbation, N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A) analysis, GLS1 expression assessment, metabolic profiling, and pharmacological validation to interrogate RNA modification-metabolism coupling in hemangioma cells. Using this framework, we examined a putative methyltransferase-like protein 16 (METTL16)-m⁶A-glutaminase 1 (GLS1) relationship associated with glutamine-related metabolic changes. METTL16 depletion markedly reduced DNA synthesis activity, with 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU)-positive cells decreasing from approximately 70% to 22-23%, and was accompanied by lower steady-state adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels. METTL16 loss was associated with decreased GLS1 mRNA m⁶A enrichment and reduced GLS1 mRNA expression to 13-18% of control levels; GLS1 promoter-reporter activity also declined. In pharmacological experiments, METTL16 overexpression partially alleviated the measured metabolite and growth-related changes associated with GLS1 inhibition. Collectively, these findings are consistent with METTL16-associated changes in GLS1 expression, RNA methylation, and glutamine-related metabolic status, although effects on GLS1 transcript decay remain to be established. Direct methylation of GLS1 by METTL16, glutamine metabolic flux, and therapeutic relevance require further investigation.

title: Tau ablation rewires brain cell programs in health and restores function in disease.
abstract: Tau is a microtubule-associated protein with diverse roles in the healthy brain but contributes to neurodegenerative disorders when dysregulated. Although tau ablation has shown protective effects in several disease models, how its absence confers this protection remains unclear. Here, we performed and analyzed single-nucleus RNA sequencing on cortices of aged tau knockout (Mapt -/- ) mice in a wild-type background as well as in a vascular amyloid model to evaluate the effect on disease context. Comparisons in a wild-type setting revealed that tau ablation induced compensatory remodeling across multiple cell types. Excitatory neurons expanded into a distinct subtype with unique glutamatergic signaling, astrocytes adopted synaptoprotective states, oligodendrocytes upregulated genes supporting connectivity and plasticity, and microglia engaged structural remodeling programs. In contrast, in disease, tau removal not only restored functions disrupted by vascular amyloid pathology, but also generated new phenotypes. Excitatory neurons rewired receptor and postsynaptic signaling; astrocytes and oligodendrocytes recovered wild-type-like gene programs related to neurotransmitter cycling, synaptic support, and myelin integrity; and microglia reprogrammed toward sensing and mounting responses. Together, these findings demonstrate that tau ablation reshapes brain cellular programs in a context-dependent manner, exerting adaptive responses in the otherwise healthy brain while restoring homeostatic functions under vascular amyloid pathology. These results position tau as a key regulator of neuronal-glial network balance and highlight the importance of understanding how tau influences distinct cellular programs within specific disease environments.

title: Palmitate Drives Mitochondrial and Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress Through Disruption of Adenosine Signaling.
abstract: Metabolic disorders associated with elevated saturated fatty acids are linked to chronic inflammatory diseases, including periodontitis, yet the mechanisms connecting lipotoxic stress to gingival inflammation remain unclear. This study investigated how palmitate-induced metabolic stress affects purinergic signaling, mitochondrial function, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in murine gingival fibroblasts (mGF), and whether adenosine modulates these effects. mGF were treated with bovine serum albumin (BSA) control, palmitate, interleukin (IL)-1β, or palmitate plus IL-1β, followed by bulk Ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, real-time extracellular flux analysis, biochemical assays, and transmission electron microscopy. Palmitate altered the expression of multiple components of purinergic adenosine signaling, including cluster of differentiation CD73 (Nt5e), CD39 (Entpd1), adenosine kinase(Adk), adenosine deaminase (Ada), and adenosine receptors. Concurrently, palmitate and IL-1β together enhanced the expression of inflammatory mediators such as C-X-C motif chemokine ligand (Cxcl)1, Cxcl2, Cxcl5, Ccl2, and Il6. Gene ontology analysis demonstrated enrichment of pathways related to innate immune activation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, ER stress, and purine metabolism. Palmitate also induced intracellular lipid accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction, evidenced by reduced Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) + /NADH ratio, increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS), elevated protein oxidation, and increased proton leak despite enhanced electron transport chain protein expression. Ultrastructural analyses revealed swollen mitochondria, ER expansion, and increased ER-mitochondrial associations. Mechanistically, palmitate activated the protein kinase R-like ER kinase (PERK)- eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2)α- activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) ER stress pathway, increasing phosphorylation of PERK and eIF2α and elevating ATF4 expression. Extracellular adenosine attenuated mitochondrial ROS accumulation, decreased PERK and ATF4 activation, improved mitochondrial respiration, and preserved ER and mitochondrial ultrastructure. Palmitate alters adenosine signaling while promoting mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and PERK-mediated ER stress in gingival fibroblasts. Adenosine signaling protects against lipotoxic-induced ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting the adenosine receptor axis as a potential regulatory pathway in metabolically driven periodontal inflammation.

title: Epigenetic memory meets transcriptional plasticity: Mechanistic perspectives from a chromatin regulatory hub in plants.
abstract: Epigenetic landscapes shape gene expression beyond the genetic code. How is epigenetic memory faithfully transmitted through cell divisions while retaining conditional transcriptional flexibility? In plants, LIKE HETEROCHROMATIN PROTEIN 1 (LHP1), for which the functional nomenclature Polycomb-beyond Composite Regulator 1 (PCR1) was recently proposed, offers a mechanistic lens for interrogating this paradox. Converging evidence, primarily from Arabidopsis thaliana, links LHP1 to DNA replication-coupled chromatin restoration, Polycomb-linked 3D genome organization, and long non-coding RNA (lncRNA)-mediated chromatin switching. Guided by this chromatin hub logic, we synthesize evidence across these interfaces and develop forward-looking models for how Polycomb memory may be maintained while permitting context-dependent transcriptional reconfiguration. We distinguish established mechanisms from cross-study inference and working hypotheses, highlighting key mechanistic gaps that remain unresolved. Across crops and woody perennials, cross-lineage observations suggest recurrent redeployment of LHP1-associated regulatory themes across developmental, environmental, and trait-associated regulatory programs while accommodating lineage-specific variation. Together, these perspectives highlight how a chromatin regulatory factor can help coordinate chromatin memory with transcriptional plasticity.

title: Picropodophyllotoxin Attenuates LPS-Induced Pulmonary Endothelial Inflammation and Lung Injury via the Nrf2/HO-1 Signaling Axis.
abstract: This investigation sought to determine whether picropodophyllotoxin (PPT)-a primary bioactive compound extracted from the roots of Podophyllum hexandrum-exerts protective effects against inflammation triggered by lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Using cultured human pulmonary artery endothelial cells (HPAECs) stimulated with LPS, we assessed the modulatory effects of PPT on heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), cyclooxygenase (COX-2), and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS). Furthermore, the impact of PPT on iNOS, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) was evaluated in LPS-challenged mice. The experimental results demonstrated that PPT upregulated HO-1 expression, blocked NF-κB activation, reduced COX-2/prostaglandin E2 and iNOS/nitric oxide (NO) production, and attenuated STAT protein phosphorylation. Additionally, PPT facilitated the nuclear translocation of Nrf2, enabling its binding to antioxidant response elements, which subsequently led to decreased IL-1β levels in LPS-exposed HPAECs. Notably, the PPT-mediated suppression of iNOS/NO was abolished when HO-1 was silenced via RNA interference. In the in vivo model, PPT markedly inhibited iNOS expression in pulmonary tissues and lowered TNF-α concentrations in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Overall, these findings demonstrate that PPT exerts anti-inflammatory and endothelial-protective effects in the pulmonary context and highlight its potential as a therapeutic candidate for acute lung injury and other pulmonary inflammatory disorders associated with endothelial dysfunction.

title: From selective phases to reversible fibers: context-dependent structural logic of biomolecular condensates.
abstract: Eukaryotic cellular organization relies on precise compartmentalization. A paradigm shift reveals that proteins with low-complexity domains (LCDs) assemble into dynamic, membraneless compartments called biomolecular condensates. Here, we compare the established "selective phase" model of the nuclear pore complex with the "reversible fiber" concept developed from selected RNA granules, proposing a context-dependent, structure-informed view of macromolecular assembly driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). We use the "Temperate Zone" as a descriptive heuristic: in selected systems, LCDs form labile, polymeric assemblies that are sufficiently stable for function yet sufficiently weak for regulation and reversal. This "virtue of weakness" can reflect an evolutionary trade-off, balancing self-assembly with safeguards against pathological transitions. Specific architectures, such as polar zippers and kinked β-sheets, can scaffold selected condensates into viscoelastic network fluids, whereas other condensates remain predominantly disordered and acquire viscoelasticity through transient sticker networks without detectable fibers. Importantly, in some systems, this tunable metastability means environmental stress or mutations can trigger pathological liquid-to-solid transitions, forming toxic aggregates; in other systems, disease can arise from failed condensate formation, altered composition, or depletion of a soluble functional pool. We present a synthesis in which deciphering this "molecular grammar" and the resulting material state is key to understanding condensate formation, physiological function, and dysregulation in condensatopathies such as neurodegeneration and cancer.

title: Enhanced cell wall digestibility and immunity in Arabidopsis through targeted modification of xylan structure by heterologous expression of acetyl xylan esterase and xylanases.
abstract: Xylan, a major component of the secondary cell wall in dicots, is often recalcitrant due to its acetylation and interaction with cellulose and lignin. To fine-tune the xylan structure and improve the processing of lignocellulosic biomass, overexpression of cell wall-degrading microbial enzymes is a viable option that can enhance cell wall properties and immunity. Here, we expressed a glycosyl hydrolase (GH10) xylanase (XYL) from Aspergillus nidulans and a carbohydrate esterase (CE) 1 acetyl xylan esterase (AXE) from Aspergillus niger, or both enzymes simultaneously (AXE/XYL), under the control of the constitutive cauliflower mosaic virus promoter (35S) and the woody-tissue-specific Populus trichocarpa GT43B promoter (WP) in Arabidopsis thaliana and studied their effects on the cell wall, saccharification properties, and biotic resistance. Transgenic WP:AXE/XYL lines exhibited an irregular xylem phenotype and compromised deposition of cell wall components, which correlated with downregulation of the responsible genes as revealed by RNA sequencing analysis. In contrast, 35S:AXE/XYL plants did not show any deformities, possibly because XYL expression was lower than in WP:AXE/XYL or due to variation in transgene expression. Biochemical analyses revealed reduced acetyl content in 35S:AXE and 35S:XYL/AXE lines, while total xylan content was increased in 35S:XYL, 35S:AXE, and 35S:XYL/AXE expressing plants. Notably, cellulose, xylan digestibility, and ethanol production were highest in the 35S:XYL/AXE line, surpassing the parental lines. Moreover, the 35S:XYL/AXE lines showed enhanced resistance to Pseudomonas syringae. Comparative RNA sequencing of xylobiose-treated and 35S:AXE/XYL plants revealed altered expression of defense-related genes. This was supported by elicitor assays, which suggested that xylo-oligosaccharides present in the 35S:XYL/AXE lines can promote the activation of immune marker genes along with increased accumulation of reactive oxygen species. In summary, simultaneous hydrolysis of the xylan backbone and its acetylation represents a promising approach to boost both lignocellulosic biomass quality and plant immunity.

title: Molecular and morphological characterization of Sarcocystis infections in muscles of red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) from Pennsylvania, USA.
abstract: Sarcocystis infections are common in many species of herbivores and carnivores, but there is no report of Sarcocystis infections in red fox (Vulpes vulpes) from the USA. Here, we identified muscular infections in 10 (47.6%) of 21 red foxes from Pennsylvania. By a combination of different methods (light microscopy, electron microscopy, and molecular) we identified more than two Sarcocystis species. By light microscopy, sarcocysts had three types of sarcocyst walls (thin without any protrusions, thick with finger like protrusions, and thick without visible protrusions). By transmission electron microscopy, one sarcocyst resembled Sarcocystis neurona. By molecular characterization using 18S ribosomal RNA (18S rRNA), mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (cox1), the internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1) surface antigen (SAG2) and protein markers such as GAPDH1, ROP21, and TUBA1, two Sarcocystis species were identified: S. neurona and S. caninum. Results indicate that the red fox is an intermediate host for S. neurona, a species causing fatal illness in horses and many other hosts in North America. Another species identified was S. caninum, which causes fatal illness in dogs.

title: Dissecting the molecular machinery of CRISPR-associated transposons.
abstract: CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs) are naturally occurring mobile genetic elements that combine programmable RNA-guided DNA recognition with transposase-mediated integration, enabling site-selective insertion of kilobase-scale DNA without nuclease-induced double-strand breaks. Current structural and biochemical knowledge can be viewed in terms of three functional modules: the transposase module, which performs DNA cleavage and strand transfer; the AAA+ ATPase TnsC, which forms a recruitment and regulatory platform; and TnsD or CRISPR effector-TniQ targeting complexes, which position this platform at selected DNA sites. Here, we synthesize recent structural and biochemical advances in target recognition, recruitment, donor-end pairing, and strand transfer. Comparisons with Tn7 and phage Mu highlight conserved transposase and ATPase functions and system-specific differences in how these components are organized and regulated. We discuss the implications of these advances for engineering programmable DNA-insertion systems and highlight unresolved questions in CAST transposition.

title: The spliceosome-cilium axis in retinitis pigmentosa: A dual-mechanism linking nuclear splicing to ciliary failure in photoreceptor degeneration.
abstract: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) caused by mutations in pre-mRNA processing factors (PRPFs) has long been classified as a spliceosomopathy, a disease of global splicing dysfunction with unexplained retinal specificity. This review synthesizes current evidence supporting a dual role for PRPF proteins in both RNA splicing and photoreceptor ciliogenesis, providing an integrated framework for understanding disease pathogenesis. The first pathogenic axis reflects the canonical nuclear activity of PRPF proteins. Pathogenic variants in PRPF31, PRPF8, and PRPF6 disrupt spliceosomal function, resulting in aberrant processing of retina-enriched transcripts, including genes encoding key components of the intraflagellar transport (IFT) machinery and ciliary architecture, such as IFT88, IFT122, and RPGRIP1. The second axis encompasses an emerging non-canonical mechanism. Beyond their established roles in pre-mRNA splicing, PRPF6, PRPF8, and PRPF31 localize to the photoreceptor basal body and connecting cilium, where they contribute directly to ciliogenesis and ciliary maintenance through mechanisms that are at least partially independent of their spliceosomal functions. Together, these complementary pathways indicate that photoreceptor degeneration in PRPF-associated RP is driven by both aberrant RNA splicing and direct disruption of ciliary structure and function. Additionally, this review highlight key unresolved questions, including the relative contribution of each pathway to disease initiation and progression, and discuss the therapeutic implications of strategies that target both splicing defects and ciliary dysfunction. Finally, it considers how this emerging framework places PRPF-associated RP at the intersection of spliceosomopathies and ciliopathies within the broader spectrum of inherited retinal disorders.

title: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus NSP14 disrupts STAT2-dependent ISGF3 assembly to suppress IFN-β signaling.
abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) is a major enteric pathogen of neonatal piglets and continues to cause serious losses in pig production. Although PEDV has been reported to inhibit host innate immunity through multiple strategies, how it modulates IFN-β-induced JAK-STAT signaling remains incompletely defined. Here, we show that PEDV attenuates IFN-β-induced antiviral signaling by inhibiting ISGF3 complex formation. Mechanistically, NSP14 primarily interacted with STAT2, and this interaction was mediated by the coiled-coil domain (CCD) of STAT2. NSP14 targeting of STAT2 reduced the interaction between STAT2 and IRF9, thereby impairing efficient ISGF3 complex assembly and suppressing IFN-β-induced antiviral transcription. These findings identify the STAT2-IRF9/ISGF3 assembly node as a target of PEDV NSP14 and define a mechanism by which NSP14 antagonizes downstream IFN-β antiviral signaling. IMPORTANCE: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) remains a major cause of severe diarrhea and death in young piglets, creating substantial losses for the swine industry. Although the virus is known to weaken the host interferon response, the mechanisms acting after interferon is produced are not fully understood. Here, we show that the PEDV protein NSP14 targets STAT2, a central component of the antiviral JAK-STAT pathway, and disrupts its association with IRF9. This prevents efficient formation of the ISGF3 transcriptional complex and reduces expression of antiviral genes. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized way in which PEDV suppresses host antiviral defenses and expand the known immune-regulatory functions of NSP14 beyond its established roles in viral RNA metabolism. Defining this virus-host interaction provides a clearer understanding of PEDV immune evasion and identifies the STAT2-IRF9/ISGF3 axis as a potential target for future antiviral strategies.

title: A Virus-like particle system based on parainfluenza virus PIV5-L for CRISPR-Cas9 and RNAi delivery.
abstract: Nucleic acid-targeting technologies based on CRISPR-Cas or small-hairpin RNA (shRNA) are essential for functional genomics and therapeutic development, yet a delivery platform that simultaneously ensures high efficiency, safety, modularity, and broad cell compatibility remains lacking. Here, we report L-VLP, a virus-like particle platform derived from a B-lymphoma-isolated strain of parainfluenza virus PIV5-L. This single-cycle, replication-deficient VLP functions as a dual-mode delivery system, capable of carrying either Cas9/sgRNA for CRISPR-mediated gene editing or shRNA for RNA interference, and achieves effective target gene knockdown or knockout in both breast cancer and B-lymphoma cells. Notably, the sgRNA or shRNA cassettes in L-VLP can be readily exchanged for any sequence of interest without altering the core vector architecture, providing a modular and versatile design. Functional assays confirm that L-VLP-mediated UBR5 silencing significantly inhibits tumor cell growth in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our work establishes L-VLP as a flexible and efficient platform for manipulating gene expression, with promising applications in both basic research and cancer target therapeutics.

title: Isoalantolactone suppresses non-small cell lung cancer progression by inducing ferroptosis through HSC70-mediated GPX4 degradation.
abstract: Isoalantolactone (IAL), a sesquiterpene lactone derived from Inula helenium L. and Inula racemosa Hook. f., exhibits anti-inflammatory and anticancer properties. This study investigated the effects of IAL against non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The anticancer activity and potential mechanisms of IAL were evaluated in A549 and H1299 cells using CCK-8 proliferation assays, colony formation assays, flow cytometry, and RNA sequencing. The molecular target of IAL was identified through Drug Affinity Responsive Target Stability (DARTS) coupled with mass spectrometry. The binding between IAL and its target, HSC70, was validated by molecular docking and surface plasmon resonance (SPR). The functional role of HSC70 was confirmed via co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) and lentiviral-mediated short hairpin RNA (shRNA) knockdown. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in subcutaneous xenograft models, with IAL administered every other day. IAL directly bound to HSC70 with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 1.07 μM and promoted glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) degradation. IAL induced hallmark features of ferroptosis, including lipid peroxidation, iron accumulation, glutathione (GSH) depletion, and oxidized glutathione (GSSG) elevation. In vitro, HSC70 knockdown abrogated IAL-induced GPX4 degradation and ferroptosis. In subcutaneous xenograft models, IAL significantly suppressed tumor growth without evident toxicity and was accompanied by HSC70/GPX4 changes consistent with the in vitro mechanism. IAL directly targets HSC70 and promotes GPX4 degradation, inducing ferroptosis in NSCLC cells. In subcutaneous xenograft models, IAL suppresses tumor growth with HSC70/GPX4 changes consistent with this mechanism and no overt toxicity at the tested doses. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of IAL.

title: FLOWERING LOCUS K and C-terminal domain phosphatase-like 1 cooperate to repress FLOWERING LOCUS C and promote flowering in Arabidopsis thaliana.
abstract: Successful plant reproduction largely relies on the timely transition to flowering, a developmental switch orchestrated by intertwined genetic regulatory networks that integrate internal and environmental cues. In Arabidopsis thaliana, a central regulator of this process is the floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC), whose expression is exquisitely modulated by components of the autonomous pathway through transcriptional and co-transcriptional mechanisms. The KH-domain protein FLOWERING LOCUS K (FLK) downregulates FLC splicing. Consequently, flk mutants flower late because of high FLC expression levels. In this study, we show that FLK functionally interacts with C-TERMINAL DOMAIN PHOSPHATASE-LIKE 1 (CPL1) to promote flowering. CPL1 dephosphorylates the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II (RNAP II), contributing to the repression of FLC transcription. In line with this, cpl1 mutants flower moderately late due to a mild increase in FLC levels. Our genetic and molecular analyses indicate that the lack of CPL1 synergistically enhances FLC expression and flowering time in the flk background. The physical interaction between FLK and CPL1 might support this scenario. We also found that, in addition to flowering, FLK and CPL1 interact in response to abiotic stress. These observations are consistent with our transcriptomic analysis and suggest the existence of additional common target genes beyond FLC. Our findings offer new perspectives on FLC co-transcriptional regulation, and the coordination between flowering and stress responses.

title: 3D Printed Trimodal Analytical Platform for Simultaneous Molecular Analysis of Protein, RNA, and DNA: A Proof of Concept for Multiclass Biomarker Analysis Applied to Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Protein, RNA, and DNA are normally quantified by separate methods, each needing its own sample preparation, reagents, and instrument, which limits multiclass biomarker analysis from small, crude samples. We developed the GPC3-Chip, a monolithic device fabricated by masked stereolithography (MSLA) 3D printing on a desktop printer. A single 20-60 μL sample is routed through three lanes that combine EDC/NHS amine-coupled antibody immunocapture of glypican 3 (GPC3), an on-chip UV photometric channel at 260 and 280 nm for RNA and DNA, and a pillar mesh architecture proposed to route components by size-dependent diffusional residence time. The GPC3 channel gave a concentration-dependent optical response with an empirical blank-based detection limit of 0.012 ng/mL and 97.2-103.4% recovery in spiked, diluted commercial serum; because antibody-free and isotype control surfaces were not tested, this response is not yet shown to be specific to GPC3 recognition. The RNA and DNA lanes agreed with Qubit measurements (r2 = 0.994 and 0.997; LOD 1.8 ng/mL), and fluorescent dextran tracers showed less than 8% overlap between lanes in buffer. In two murine hepatocellular carcinoma models, the GPC3 channel response exceeded the detection threshold about eight days before tumors were palpable, and the combined GPC3, cfDNA, and RNA integrity readout gave an apparent AUC of 0.987 versus 0.922 for GPC3 alone (estimated in the same samples used to build the model, without cross-validation or an independent validation set). The chip is a proof of concept, low-cost route to concentration-dependent protein and nucleic acid readouts in a single device. Specificity of the GPC3 response, independent validation of the diagnostic model, separation of real biomolecules in complex matrices, RNA and DNA selectivity in mixtures, and performance in human samples remain to be validated.

title: Structure-Guided Design of Exogenous Spike-in Controls Improves Analytical Precision in RT-qPCR-Based Small RNA Quantification.
abstract: Accurate reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR)-based quantification of circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) is limited by workflow-dependent bias arising from RNA extraction, enzymatic cDNA synthesis, amplification, matrix-derived inhibition, and sequence-dependent behavior of short RNA targets. Conventional exogenous spike-ins monitor technical process variation but are often selected without considering target-specific physicochemical properties such as GC content and predicted 3'-end structure. Here, we introduce a structure-guided framework for selecting and designing exogenous spike-in controls in small RNA quantification workflows. Native, sequence-modified, and newly engineered synthetic spike-ins were evaluated across no-extraction, pre-extraction, and post-extraction conditions, including an ethanol inhibition challenge. Secondary-structure prediction and calibration-curve-based quantification were combined with workflow-resolved coefficient of variation (CV) and ΔCq analyses. Control performance varied with the target miRNA, assay configuration, and workflow condition, with significant control, workflow, or interaction effects in selected target-assay combinations. Direct modification of predicted 3'-end structure revealed context-dependent effects on normalization precision, including a significant variant-dependent difference under the ethanol challenge, and circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy of the hsa-miR-146a-5p variant set provided experimental support for the predicted stability differences. Finally, four engineered spike-ins spanning contrasting GC/ΔG profiles were evaluated as proof-of-concept controls for a target-informed selection framework. This study provides a measurement-focused strategy for technical internal-standard design and supports assay- and workflow-specific validation of exogenous spike-in controls in complex biofluid workflows.

title: SPRINT-Cas12a: A Single Leading-Hairpin Probe-Enabled Dual-Pathway Activation Strategy for Sensitive miRNA Detection.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a possesses robust trans-cleavage activity and has emerged as a powerful tool for nucleic acid detection. However, the efficient integration of Cas12a trans-cleavage with direct miRNA recognition and signal amplification remains challenging, particularly because conventional assay designs often rely on multiple probes or a single activation pathway. Here, we developed SPRINT-Cas12a, a single-probe RNA-triggered integrated trans-cleavage platform for sensitive miRNA detection. In this design, a leading hairpin probe (L-HP) specifically recognizes the target miRNA and initiates polymerase-mediated cascade isothermal amplification, synchronously generating two structurally distinct Cas12a-activating products: an RNA-DNA complex and a long-chain micro-hairpin probe (L-MHP). These products provide complementary activation pathways for Cas12a, thereby promoting reporter cleavage and fluorescence signal generation. The single-probe architecture simplifies probe design while enabling synergistic signal amplification through dual-pathway Cas12a activation. The platform was successfully adapted for the detection of miR-21 and miR-122, two miRNAs with distinct sequences, demonstrating its modularity and sequence versatility. Using miR-192 as a hepatocellular carcinoma-associated target, the method achieved sensitive detection in serum samples and distinguished patients with hepatocellular carcinoma from healthy controls, with results consistent with stem-loop quantitative reverse-transcription PCR. In addition, the platform was coupled with a lateral flow assay to provide an instrument-free visual readout. Depending on the amplification and readout format, the assay could be completed within 90 min to 120 min using simple laboratory equipment. Overall, SPRINT-Cas12a provides a single-probe, dual-pathway strategy for Cas12a-mediated miRNA detection and shows promise for portable molecular diagnostics and point-of-care testing.

title: The hDPSC-CM-derived peptide P1DC promotes osteogenic differentiation by regulating the p38/MAPK pathway.
abstract: Human dental pulp stem cells (hDPSCs) are dental-derived mesenchymal stem cells with robust multipotent differentiation potential, indicating that they are promising for bone tissue engineering (BTE). We previously screened a secreted peptide, P1DC, derived from differentiated hDPSC-CM, that markedly promoted the proliferation of hDPSCs. However, its effect on osteogenesis and bone regeneration is unknown. HDPSCs were isolated from dental pulp tissue. The effects of P1DC on the osteogenic activity of hDPSCs were evaluated by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‒PCR), western blotting, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) staining, and Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining. Additionally, the role of P1DC in bone formation in vivo was validated in a rat calvarial defect model. Micro-CT, hematoxylin-eosin, Masson's trichrome staining and immunohistochemistry were used to verify the effects of P1DC on bone regeneration. Moreover, RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) analysis was performed to analyze the underlying mechanisms of P1DC-induced osteogenesis. In hDPSCs, 2.5 µM P1DC significantly upregulated the mRNA and protein levels of osteogenic markers (Runx2, ALP, and OSX), increased ALP activity, and accelerated matrix mineralization, with all differences statistically significant (p < 0.05). Furthermore, micro-CT analyses in vivo rat calvarial defect models revealed that 2.5 μM P1DC markedly augmented bone regeneration capacity (p < 0.05). Hematoxylin‒eosin and Masson's trichrome staining also verified substantially more mature bone matrix deposition within P1DC-treated group, with significantly higher new bone area fraction (p < 0.05). Mechanistically, RNA-sequencing profiling indicated activation of the MAPK signaling pathway following P1DC treatment. Further Western blot validation revealed markedly elevated phosphorylation levels of p38 in P1DC-treated hDPSCs (p < 0.05), and the osteogenic differentiation of P1DC + p38 inhibitor group was statistically inferior to that of the P1DC single-treatment group (p < 0.05). Collectively, our results indicated that P1DC effectively increased osteogenic differentiation in hDPSCs in vitro and facilitated bone regeneration in vivo, at least partially via the p38/MAPK signaling pathway, suggesting new avenues for enhancing bone regeneration strategies.

title: A novel ultra-rare nonsense variant linked to PCDHGC4-related neurodevelopmental disorder in an Iranian patient.
abstract: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in PCDHGC4 cause a rare autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmental delay or intellectual disability, severe speech impairment, gait abnormalities, and variably microcephaly, seizures, and joint anomalies. The transcript-level consequence of premature termination variants is important because nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) may preclude production of a stable truncated protein. We clinically evaluated a 9-year-old Iranian Sistani boy and performed whole-exome sequencing followed by Sanger validation and segregation analysis. Variant nomenclature and exon architecture were verified against the MANE Select transcript NM_018928.3. NMD was assessed using canonical exon-junction-complex rules and the UCSC NMDetective-AI track. The patient had moderate intellectual disability, absent speech, esotropic strabismus, delayed walking, and a persistent wide-based unsteady gait, without seizures, microcephaly, or joint hypermobility at the most recent assessment. Brain MRI showed symmetric peritrigonal white-matter hyperintensities without a major structural anomaly. A novel homozygous NM_018928.3:c.1369 C > T variant was identified in PCDHGC4; codon-level validation corrected the protein consequence to NP_061751.1:p.(Gln457Ter). The premature termination codon lies in exon 1 of 4, 1071 nucleotides upstream of the first downstream exon-exon junction and 1219 nucleotides upstream of the final junction. Canonical rules therefore predict NMD sensitivity, whereas NMDetective-AI yielded an intermediate/uncertain score (-0.1644), close to its NMD-evading threshold. This additional family expands the phenotypic and allelic spectrum of PCDHGC4-related neurodevelopmental disorder. The most defensible current mechanism is loss of function, with NMD predicted by the canonical positional rule but not experimentally confirmed. Patient-derived RNA studies are required to determine NMD efficiency and whether any truncated protein is produced.

title: Identification of translation events that drive nonsense-mediated mRNA decay reveals functional roles for alternative RNA isoforms.
abstract: The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway targets mRNAs undergoing premature translation termination for degradation. Previously, RNA-seq of yeast lacking NMD revealed that most genes targeted by NMD lack obvious premature termination codons (PTCs). We develop a combined approach using RNA-seq and 40S ribosome profiling to identify cryptic premature termination events that could account for NMD on nearly all these transcripts, including many alternative RNA transcript isoforms associated with annotated genes. Many NMD-targeted transcripts appear to be involved in two-promoter gene regulatory systems and share properties with long un-decoded transcript isoforms (LUTIs). In particular, we show that the DAL5 LUTI regulates expression of the DAL5 protein-coding mRNA in response to changes to environmental nitrogen. Our work expands the functional roles for LUTIs and establishes the importance of NMD in their regulation.

title: Black-White disparities in HIV care continuum outcomes: contribution of social and structural determinants of health.
abstract: Despite advances in HIV care and treatment, disparities persist among racially minoritized populations. We evaluated the extent to which social and structural determinants of health (SDOH) account for Black-White differences in HIV care continuum outcomes. We performed a retrospective analysis using the Johns Hopkins HIV Clinical Cohort, which prospectively collects data including SDOH and clinical outcomes on individuals engaged in care at an HIV clinic in Baltimore, Maryland. We included non-Hispanic Black and White participants with at least one HIV primary care visit in 2023. We assessed three outcomes in 2024: at least one missed visit, at least one viral load measurement, and viral load nonsuppression (≥1 HIV RNA ≥200 copies/mL). We estimated racial differences using linear and modified Poisson regression with sequential adjustment for covariates. SDOH included individual-level factors (income, housing, and health insurance) and census block group-level socioeconomic deprivation. Of 1538 participants, 1240 (81%) were Black and 298 (19%) were White. Black participants had higher rates of missed visits (55 vs. 25%); this was attenuated by two-thirds after SDOH adjustment [risk difference 0.10, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.02, 0.17]. Viral load measurement was similar between groups (91 vs. 89%). Black participants had higher rates of viral load nonsuppression (9 vs. 3%); this was also attenuated after SDOH adjustment (risk difference 0.03, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.07). Racial differences in missed visits and viral load nonsuppression were attenuated after accounting for SDOH. These findings highlight the important link between SDOH and racial disparities across multiple stages of the HIV care continuum.

title: Identification of the Anti-Inflammatory Metabolite Kynurenine as a New Substrate of the Transport Protein OATP3A1.
abstract: Kynurenine, the major metabolite of tryptophan, plays a crucial role during inflammatory processes. By activating the aryl hydrocarbon receptor kynurenine exhibits anti-inflammatory effects in several diseases such as the inflammatory bowel diseases ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Adverse outcomes of Crohn's disease patients were associated with a single nucleotide polymorphism, localized in the gene SLCO3A1 encoding the transport protein organic anion transporting polypeptide (OATP) 3A1. OATP3A1 is ubiquitously expressed throughout the human body and was recently shown to mediate transport of the amino acids tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine. Our goal was to characterize kynurenine as a substrate of OATP3A1 and to extend the knowledge about this transporter in the context of inflammatory processes. HEK293 cells stably overexpressing OATP3A1 and respective control cells were used in combination with an LC-MS-based untargeted metabolomics approach, uptake studies, and metabolic flux analyses. We identified kynurenine as a substrate of OATP3A1 and determined kinetic transport parameters (K m and V max value) as 133 ± 40 µM and 1863 ± 154 pmol/mg protein/min, respectively. RNA-sequencing data (IBDome database) showed elevated SLCO3A1 expression in colon tissue of patients with inflammatory bowel diseases, which was particularly evident in the inflamed tissue of ulcerative colitis patients. Additionally, SLCO3A1 mRNA expression in primary human blood-derived and ex vivo-stimulated CD4+ T lymphocytes was induced by addition of kynurenine, regardless of whether the aryl hydrocarbon receptor antagonist CH223191 was added. In summary, we characterized kynurenine as a substrate of OATP3A1, which showed elevated RNA expression in ulcerative colitis. Moreover, kynurenine induced SLCO3A1 mRNA expression in primary human CD4+ T lymphocytes.

title: IEPA scavenges reactive carbonyl species to mitigate oxidative stress in a rat model of acute radiation syndrome and modulates irradiation-induced transcriptomic changes.
abstract: Exposure to high doses of ionizing radiation may cause acute radiation syndrome (ARS), in which reactive oxygen and carbonyl species (ROS/RCS) and DNA damage contribute to cell death and depletion of bone marrow and peripheral blood cells. Although recombinant growth factor therapies reduce mortality in preclinical models, their reliance on parenteral administration may limit their utility in mass-casualty scenarios. Imidazolyl ethanamide pentandioic acid (IEPA) is an orally bioavailable small molecule that improves survival in rodent models of ARS. While in vitro data suggest an antioxidant mechanism, its mode of action in vivo remains incompletely understood. Mechanistic studies were conducted in female WAG/RijCmcr rats exposed to 7.75 Gy total-body irradiation (TBI). Systemic oxidative stress was assessed by quantifying reduced glutathione levels in blood. Urine from IEPA-treated animals was analyzed by LC-MS/MS for metabolites indicative of RCS scavenging. Protein carbonylation was evaluated in vitro by Western blot. Transcriptomic alterations associated with IEPA treatment were characterized by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of bone marrow and peripheral blood samples collected on days 4 and 14 post-TBI. IEPA increased reduced glutathione levels in the blood of irradiated rats by 21% (p = .035). A product of the direct scavenging reaction between IEPA and the prevalent RCS 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) was detected in urine. IEPA reduced 4-HNE-mediated protein carbonylation in vitro. In addition, IEPA treatment was associated with transcriptomic changes (132 differentially expressed genes with fold change > 2, p.adj < 0.05) particularly in the peripheral blood on day 14 post-TBI. Gene ontology analysis indicated modulation of immune cell differentiation. IEPA attenuated irradiation-induced systemic oxidative stress, potentially in part through direct scavenging of RCS. Associated transcriptomic changes suggest modulation of immune differentiation pathways in peripheral blood. This warrants further study of RCS scavenging, oxidative stress reduction and immunomodulation in IEPA treatment in the future.

title: A Structurally Dynamic Chromosome 11 Locus from Oryza rufipogon Confers Recessive Resistance to Bacterial Blight in Rice.
abstract: Bacterial blight (BB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), poses a major threat to global rice production as rapidly evolving pathogen populations overcome existing resistance genes. In this study, we characterized genetic resistance in the Oryza rufipogon accession Wild-173 (UP36), which exhibited broad resistance to diverse Xoo strains, whereas the susceptible cultivar Longjing-31 (LG31) displayed severe disease symptoms. Genetic analysis of an F2 population derived from UP36♂×LG31♀ indicated that BB resistance is controlled by a recessive locus, consistent with a 1:3 (R: S) segregation ratio (χ2 test, P > 0.05). Bulked segregant analysis coupled with whole-genome resequencing (BSA-seq) identified a significant G' peak on chromosome 11. Fine mapping using InDel markers delimited the locus to an approximately 34 kb interval flanked by markers bb94 and bb26 on the long arm of chromosome 11. Within this interval, nine candidate genes were predicted. Two genes encoding a calmodulin-binding protein and an EAP30/Vps36 domain-containing protein showed sequence variation between UP36 and LG31 and were designated xa53-1(t) and xa53-2(t), while the remaining candidates were primarily retrotransposon-related. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of both candidate genes in a susceptible cultivar resulted in reduced lesion lengths, providing functional evidence for their roles in BB resistance. A high-quality PacBio HiFi assembly of UP36 revealed substantial structural variation and sequence divergence, including presence/absence polymorphisms and disrupted collinearity, indicating that this locus is distinct from previously cloned Xa genes. RNA-seq analysis of UP36 and LG31 following Xoo inoculation prioritized candidate genes and revealed transcriptional reprogramming associated with defense signaling, stress responses, and hormone-mediated immunity. Consistently, qPCR analysis showed stronger induction of defense-related marker genes (PR1a, PR1b, PR5, and PBZ1) in UP36 compared with LG31 after Xoo inoculation. Together, these findings demonstrate that UP36 harbors a novel recessive resistance locus on chromosome 11 conferring broad-spectrum BB resistance and provide valuable genomic resources for gene cloning and resistance breeding.

title: Hepatitis C virus remodels lipid droplets to promote mitochondrial fatty acid accumulation and metabolic activation.
abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) depends on host lipid metabolism and lipid droplets (LDs) for genome replication, assembly, and particle production, yet how LD structure and lipid utilization change over the course of infection remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the temporal remodeling of LD-associated metabolic pathways during HCV JFH-1 infection of human hepatoma Huh7 cells. HCV infection transiently increased LD fluorescence intensity at 24 h post-infection (hpi), followed by normalization or relative loss of LD signal at later time points. Concomitantly, LDs became progressively clustered and enlarged during late infection, despite reduced protein levels of the canonical LD fusion proteins CIDEA, CIDEB, and CIDEC, suggesting that HCV-induced LD enlargement is not associated with increased expression of CIDE proteins. Transcriptomic, RT-qPCR, and immunoblot analyses revealed time-dependent regulation of genes and proteins involved in LD structure, triglyceride synthesis, lipolysis, lipid uptake, and mitochondrial fatty acid utilization. Subcellular fractionation demonstrated preferential accumulation of fatty acids in mitochondrial fractions at 24-72 hpi. This redistribution was accompanied by increased oxygen consumption rate, elevated extracellular acidification, and progressive reactive oxygen species accumulation, indicating infection-associated metabolic activation and oxidative stress. Pharmacological inhibition of DGAT1-dependent LD biogenesis, LIPA-dependent lysosomal lipid hydrolysis, LIPE/HSL-dependent lipolysis, or CPT1-dependent mitochondrial fatty acid transport markedly reduced mitochondrial fatty acid accumulation and suppressed HCV-induced respiratory activity. Inhibition of LIPA or LIPE/HSL reduced both HCV RNA and core protein levels, whereas inhibition of CPT1 or DGAT1 had more pronounced effects on core protein than on viral RNA. Together, these findings support a model in which HCV dynamically remodels LDs, mobilizes LD-associated fatty acids, and redirects them toward mitochondria to support infection-associated metabolism and downstream stages of the viral life cycle. Lipid hydrolysis and mitochondrial fatty acid trafficking therefore represent potential host-directed targets for limiting HCV infection.IMPORTANCEHepatitis C virus depends on host lipid metabolism for replication, assembly, and production of infectious particles, but how it uses lipid droplets over time remains incompletely understood. This study shows that hepatitis C virus dynamically remodels lipid droplets, causing an early increase in lipid storage followed by droplet enlargement and mobilization of fatty acids during later infection. The released fatty acids preferentially accumulate in mitochondria, where they are associated with increased cellular respiration and oxidative stress. Blocking lipid droplet formation, lipid breakdown, or fatty acid transport to mitochondria reduced this metabolic response and decreased viral RNA or core protein accumulation. Inhibition of lysosomal acid lipase and hormone-sensitive lipase suppressed both viral RNA and protein levels. These findings identify lipid droplet breakdown and mitochondrial fatty acid trafficking as important host processes used by hepatitis C virus and as potential targets for host-directed antiviral intervention.

title: Changes in the chromatin accessibility landscape during human adenovirus infection.
abstract: Viral infections rewire the cellular environment, and this is often achieved through chromatin remodeling. Human adenovirus (HAdV) can directly modify specific cellular chromatin features; however, we still lack a global view of the changes in the cellular chromatin landscape induced during infection. To address how host chromatin accessibility changes during HAdV-C5 infection, we performed assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) in growth-arrested diploid human lung fibroblast (IMR-90) cells at 48 and 72 h post-infection. We detected widespread changes in chromatin accessibility, with 7,055 and 10,736 differentially accessible regions (DARs) on host chromatin at 48 and 72 h post-infection, respectively. At both time points, these changes mostly occurred in enhancer/intergenic regions and intronic regions. Furthermore, the pattern of changes in accessibility differed between protein-coding and non-coding genes. Integration of the ATAC-seq data with RNA-seq data demonstrated that significant changes in chromatin accessibility coincided with significant changes in gene expression during infection. Additionally, we found that increased DARs were enriched for forkhead and TEA domain transcription factor family motifs, while decreased DARs were enriched for motifs from zinc finger and basic leucine zipper domain families. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that Wnt signaling pathway genes displayed increased chromatin accessibility during infection. Inhibition of the Wnt signaling pathway reduced viral gene expression and infectious viral progeny production, suggesting that this pathway is important for productive infection. Together, these data demonstrate that cellular chromatin is extensively remodeled during HAdV infection and expand our understanding of host-cell transcriptional regulation by human adenovirus. Human adenovirus-C5 (HAdV-C5) infection extensively modifies the cellular transcriptome and proteome. However, other important aspects of the cellular environment, such as global changes in chromatin accessibility, have yet to be fully characterized during infection. Here, we performed assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) in infected growth-arrested diploid human lung fibroblast (IMR-90) cells at 48 and 72 h post-infection. We observed genome-wide changes in cellular chromatin accessibility and identified specific transcription factor motifs located in differentially accessible regions during infection. This work contributes another key piece to our understanding of how human adenovirus infection reprograms the host-cell environment and will inform future work directed toward specific chromatin modifications manipulated by HAdV that impact host-cell chromatin accessibility.

title: Transcriptomic data and biomedical literature synergize in finding pharmacologic gene regulators.
abstract: Most disorders caused by a deficiency or excess of one gene product lack targeted therapies. Since these disorders can be modeled with a gene overexpression, knockout, or knockdown, drugs that oppose the transcriptomic effects of such perturbations may be promising therapeutic candidates. RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) studies can fuel this drug-prioritization, but their labels, written in plain language, must be annotated manually. Hence, we introduce Signature-based Networks from Automatically Curated Knockout, Knockdown, and Small-molecule Studies (SNACKKSS), which automatically curates gene-disruption and drug-treatment studies from the Gene Expression Omnibus and, in partnership with uniformly computed read count datasets, feeds the labels and RNA-seq data directly into regulatory relationship predictions. Through cross-validation, we show that the predictions from SNACKKSS (specifically, from a variant called "SA4") make a unique contribution to finding protein-inhibiting compounds, even alongside existing predictors. We demonstrate the benefit of aggregating multiple predictive tools, and provide this powerful ensemble alongside SNACKKSS. Importantly, we advise researchers to test complex machine learning models on multiple devices, since the hardware architecture can affect their output. Nonetheless, our findings support the value of integrating automatically curated RNA-seq signatures with literature- and co-expression-based predictors for drug-repurposing prioritization.

title: Remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment and underlying oncogenic molecular mechanisms in HPV-associated OSCC.
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) possesses unique clinical and biological characteristics, while its specific clinicopathological features and underlying immune-molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to systematically characterize the clinicopathological traits of HPV-associated OSCC and elucidate the key molecular and immune regulatory axes driving its malignant progression. We retrospectively analyzed the correlations between HPV infection status and multiple clinical parameters including age, gender, primary tumor location, clinical stage, pathological grade, and 5-year overall survival (OS) in OSCC patients. IHC was performed to detect the protein expression levels of p53, Cyclin D1 and pRb in OSCC tumor tissues, while flow cytometry was used to quantify the infiltration levels of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and regulatory T cells (Tregs) in paired tumor tissues and peripheral blood specimens. Integrated transcriptomic RNA sequencing, miRNA target prediction and bioinformatic analyses were further conducted to screen core oncogenic immune targets and specific regulatory pathways in HPV-positive OSCC. Significant differences in primary tumor site, pathological differentiation and 5-year OS were identified between HPV-positive and HPV-negative OSCC patients, with no notable differences in age, gender and clinical stage across groups. And HPV-positive OSCC tissues presented markedly downregulated p53 and Cyclin D1 expression compared with the HPV-negative counterpart. MDSC levels progressively increased from controls to patients with oral precancerous lesions and OSCC, whereas Treg levels were significantly elevated in OSCC patients compared with both controls and patients with precancerous lesions. Bioinformatic analysis revealed that Calsequestrin 2 (CASQ2) expression was negatively correlated with tumor purity in HPV-positive OSCC, and two core circRNA-miRNA regulatory axes (hsa_circ_0058495/hsa-miR-2115-5p and hsa_circ_0032029/hsa-miR-2115-5p) were identified to target CASQ2 specifically. Collectively, HPV infection remodels the OSCC tumor microenvironment into an immunosuppressive phenotype via inducing abnormal accumulation of MDSCs and Tregs, thereby promoting OSCC malignant progression. The miRNA-mediated CASQ2 dysregulation may serve as a core pathogenic driver of HPV-positive OSCC. These findings uncover a novel immune-molecular mechanism underlying HPV-associated OSCC progression, and provide a theoretical basis for stratified precision immunotherapy for this unique OSCC subtype.

title: Early Brucella abortus infection reshapes the exosomal lncRNA cargo of macrophages and highlights putative immunoregulatory pathways.
abstract: Brucella abortus is an intracellular pathogen that profoundly alters macrophage responses, but the contribution and extracellular distribution of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) during infection remain poorly characterized. Here, we characterized the exosomal lncRNA landscape of B. abortus-infected RAW 264.7 macrophages and applied an integrated bioinformatic framework to prioritize candidate lncRNAs and their potential functional contexts. Exosomes were isolated from infected and control macrophages at 8 h post-infection, and their RNA content was analyzed by high-throughput sequencing. Differential expression analysis identified 83 lncRNAs with altered expression, with most showing reduced expression in exosomes from infected cells. Functional enrichment analysis of protein-coding genes located within ±250 kb of the differentially expressed lncRNAs generated associations with immune-related processes, including antigen presentation and cytotoxicity, as well as ion transport, lipid metabolism, and lymphocyte-related processes.
